basic.q: Which Part of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Rights?
basic.e: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III (Articles 12–35) of the Constitution.

basic.q: Fundamental Rights are covered under which range of Articles?
Which Article defines the term 'State' for the purposes of Part III?
basic.e: Article 12 defines 'State' to include the Government and Parliament of India, State Legislatures, local authorities, and other authorities.

basic.q: Which Article declares that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void?
basic.e: Article 13 voids any law (pre- or post-Constitution) that is inconsistent with or takes away Fundamental Rights.

o: Equality before law and equal protection of laws
basic.e: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to all persons.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form; it is a punishable offence.

basic.q: Which Article abolishes titles (except military and academic distinctions)?
basic.e: Article 18 abolishes titles; the State cannot confer titles other than military or academic distinctions.

basic.q: How many freedoms are currently guaranteed under Article 19(1) after the 44th Amendment?
basic.e: Originally seven freedoms were listed; the right to property [19(1)(f)] was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978), leaving six freedoms.

basic.q: Which Article protects a person against ex-post-facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination?
basic.e: Article 20 covers protection in respect of conviction for offences — no ex-post-facto law, no double jeopardy, and no self-incrimination.

basic.q: Which Article guarantees 'Protection of life and personal liberty'?
basic.e: Article 21 states no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

basic.q: Article 21A, guaranteeing the Right to Education, was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment?
basic.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, providing free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years.

basic.q: Which Article prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar)?
basic.e: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour (begar).

basic.q: Which Article prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or hazardous work?
basic.e: Article 24 bars employment of children below 14 years in hazardous occupations.

basic.q: Which Article did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
basic.e: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) was described by Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

basic.q: Which Article empowers Parliament to restrict Fundamental Rights in their application to the armed forces?
basic.e: Article 33 allows Parliament to modify FRs' application to armed forces, para-military, and intelligence personnel.

intermediate.q: Which clause of Article 15 was added by the 103rd Amendment to allow reservation based on economic criteria (EWS)?
intermediate.e: Article 15(6), inserted by the 103rd Amendment (2019), permits up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections.

intermediate.q: 'Cooperative societies' was added to the freedom under Article 19(1)(c) by which Amendment?
intermediate.e: The 97th Amendment Act, 2011 added the right to form 'cooperative societies' to Article 19(1)(c).

intermediate.q: Which writ is issued by a court to release a person illegally detained?
intermediate.e: Habeas Corpus ('to have the body') commands that a detained person be produced before the court to examine the legality of detention.

intermediate.q: Which writ is issued to command a public official or authority to perform a duty they have failed to perform?
intermediate.e: Mandamus ('we command') directs a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed or refused to perform.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is a correct distinction between Article 32 and Article 226?
o: Article 226 is a Fundamental Right, Article 32 is not
Article 32 (Supreme Court) is limited to enforcement of Fundamental Rights, while Article 226 (High Courts) extends to any other legal right as well
Only High Courts can issue writs
Article 32 can be suspended by an ordinary law
intermediate.e: Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right restricted to enforcing Part III rights; Article 226 gives High Courts wider power covering FRs and other legal rights, but is not itself a Fundamental Right.

intermediate.q: Under Article 22, for how long can a person be detained without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board (in ordinary preventive detention law, pre-2019 practice)?
intermediate.e: Ordinarily, preventive detention beyond 3 months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board, per Article 22(4).

intermediate.q: After the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Part III, under which Article does it survive as a mere legal right?
intermediate.e: Right to property is now a constitutional legal right (not a Fundamental Right) under Article 300A.

intermediate.q: Reservation for backward classes in public employment is provided under which Article?
intermediate.e: Article 16(4) enables the State to reserve appointments/posts for backward classes not adequately represented in services.

intermediate.q: Which Articles collectively guarantee the 'Right to Freedom of Religion'?
intermediate.e: Articles 25 to 28 cover freedom of conscience, religious practice, managing religious affairs, freedom from religious taxes, and religious instruction.

intermediate.q: Which Article ensures the State cannot levy taxes to promote or maintain any particular religion?
intermediate.e: Article 27 ensures no person is compelled to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion.

intermediate.q: The right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice is given to minorities under which Article?
intermediate.e: Article 30 grants minorities (religious or linguistic) the right to establish and administer educational institutions.

intermediate.q: Which of these Fundamental Rights is available only to citizens, NOT to foreigners?
intermediate.e: Article 19 freedoms are available only to citizens. Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23 and 25 are available to all persons, citizens or not.

intermediate.q: The maximum ceiling on total reservations set by the Supreme Court (with certain exceptions) is:
intermediate.e: In Indra Sawhney v Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court capped reservations at 50%, barring extraordinary circumstances.

intermediate.q: Which Article deals with the 'Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases'?
intermediate.e: Article 22 lays down procedural safeguards for arrested/detained persons, and also covers preventive detention.

intermediate.q: Which Article empowers only Parliament (not State Legislatures) to make laws giving effect to certain Fundamental Rights, like punishing untouchability under Article 17?
intermediate.e: Article 35 reserves to Parliament alone the power to legislate on specified matters under Part III, including prescribing punishment for Article 17 and 23 violations.

advanced.q: The 'Basic Structure Doctrine' of the Constitution was propounded in which landmark case?
o: A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v Union of India
advanced.e: In Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973), a 13-judge bench held Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter its 'basic structure'.

advanced.q: Which case significantly expanded the scope of Article 21, holding that the 'procedure established by law' must be right, just and fair, not arbitrary?
o: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978)
advanced.e: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) overturned the narrow view from A.K. Gopalan, ruling that any procedure depriving life/liberty must be fair, just and reasonable — linking Articles 14, 19 and 21 (the 'Golden Triangle').

advanced.q: The Right to Privacy was declared a Fundamental Right under which case, and under which Article?
advanced.e: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017), a 9-judge bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a Fundamental Right protected under Article 21.

advanced.q: The 'Golden Triangle' of the Indian Constitution refers to which combination of Articles?
advanced.e: The 'Golden Triangle' refers to Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms) and 21 (life and liberty), which courts read together to test the validity of laws.

advanced.q: In which case did the Supreme Court read down Section 377 of the IPC, decriminalising consensual homosexual acts between adults?
o: Joseph Shine v Union of India
Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India
Shayara Bano v Union of India
advanced.e: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (2018) held that Section 377 IPC, insofar as it criminalised consensual sexual acts between adults of the same sex, violated Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21.

advanced.q: The practice of 'instant triple talaq' (talaq-e-biddat) was declared unconstitutional in which case?
o: Shayara Bano v Union of India (2017)
advanced.e: Shayara Bano v Union of India (2017) struck down instant triple talaq as unconstitutional and arbitrary, violating Article 14.

advanced.q: Section 497 IPC (criminalising adultery) was struck down as unconstitutional in which case?
o: Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018)
Lata Singh v State of UP
Independent Thought v Union of India
advanced.e: Joseph Shine v Union of India (2018) struck down Section 497 IPC, holding it violated Articles 14, 15 and 21 by treating women as property of their husbands.

advanced.q: In A.K. Gopalan v State of Madras (1950), the Supreme Court interpreted Article 21 in which manner?
o: Broad and purposive, linking it to Articles 14 and 19
Narrow/literal — any procedure enacted by a validly made law was sufficient, regardless of fairness
As including the right to privacy
advanced.e: The early A.K. Gopalan ruling took a literal view: as long as a 'procedure established by law' existed, it need not be fair — a position later reversed by Maneka Gandhi (1978).

advanced.q: Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980) is significant because it held that:
o: Fundamental Rights can never be amended
There must be a harmonious balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles; unlimited power to amend FRs for DPSPs is unconstitutional
Directive Principles are superior to Fundamental Rights in all cases
Right to Property is a Fundamental Right
advanced.e: Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment that gave Parliament unlimited amending power over FRs to implement DPSPs, holding the harmony/balance between Part III and Part IV is part of the basic structure.

advanced.q: Which case first held that Parliament CANNOT amend Fundamental Rights at all — a position later overruled by Kesavananda Bharati?
o: I.C. Golaknath v State of Punjab (1967)
advanced.e: Golaknath v State of Punjab (1967) held Fundamental Rights are beyond the amending power of Parliament under Article 368; this rigid view was overruled by Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which introduced the basic structure test instead.

advanced.q: The concept of 'creamy layer' exclusion in OBC reservations was introduced through which case?
o: Indra Sawhney v Union of India (1992)
M. Nagaraj v Union of India (2006)
Jarnail Singh v Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018)
Ashoka Kumar Thakur v Union of India (2008)
advanced.e: Indra Sawhney v Union of India (1992) (Mandal case) introduced the 'creamy layer' concept to exclude the socially advanced among backward classes from reservation benefits.

advanced.q: Article 16(4A), permitting reservation in promotions for SC/STs, was examined for validity in which case?
o: M. Nagaraj v Union of India (2006)
advanced.e: M. Nagaraj v Union of India (2006) upheld the validity of Article 16(4A) but required the State to show backwardness, inadequate representation, and administrative efficiency data — conditions later eased in Jarnail Singh (2018).

advanced.q: Which case is considered the origin of India's earliest Fundamental Rights amendment controversy, prompting the 1st Amendment (1951)?
o: Champakam Dorairajan v State of Madras
advanced.e: State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan (1951), which struck down caste-based reservation as violating Article 29(2), led to the 1st Amendment inserting Article 15(4).

advanced.q: Which statement about Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (per Minerva Mills and subsequent rulings) is most accurate?
o: Fundamental Rights are always subordinate to Directive Principles
Directive Principles can never influence interpretation of Fundamental Rights
Neither is absolutely superior; courts strive for harmonious construction, and the balance itself is part of the basic structure
Directive Principles are fully justiciable like Fundamental Rights
advanced.e: Courts (notably in Minerva Mills) hold that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles must be balanced harmoniously — neither is completely subordinate, and this balance is itself part of the Constitution's basic structure.

advanced.q: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019), introducing EWS reservation, added which two clauses?
advanced.e: The 103rd Amendment (2019) inserted Article 15(6) and Article 16(6), enabling up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections in education and public employment.
